hook_text: Same mine, same shaft. One worker earns ten times more than the man beside him. Why?
clip_script: The Rand, around 1900. A Cornish miner who knows how to blast and timber earns top wages and belongs to a union. Beside him, a black worker drills by hand for a fraction of the pay. When the mine owners try to give black workers skilled jobs to cut costs, white workers demand a colour bar: these jobs are for whites only. Meanwhile, Afrikaner families who lost their farms to rinderpest, drought and war crowd into Johannesburg, poor and unskilled. The owners prefer cheap labour and bring in sixty-three thousand Chinese workers. And in Natal and the Transvaal, Indian South Africans face law after law: land limits, a three-pound tax, no vote, fingerprints. These divisions were not natural. They were made.
visual_style: A whiteboard mine split into labelled jobs with a bar drawn across, then a farm wagon heading to a city, a ship from China, and a stack of law documents stamped 1885, 1891, 1895, 1896, 1897 and 1907.
pacing: Brisk, one group every few seconds, ending on the stack of laws.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson to see how the divisions were built.
